positions.source_passage: Postmarket monitoring should additionally verify continued compliance with the assumptions used in the Criticality Stratification, including the actual effectiveness of human oversight, scope limitations, escalation procedures, and other safeguards.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that periodic re-benchmarking could be treated as a substitute for genuine postmarket clinical performance evaluation, and that monitoring focused on model outputs alone would miss how the device performs in real clinical workflows.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should treat re-benchmarking, sample-based clinician review, and degradation monitoring as complementary rather than interchangeable, and, depending on criticality, expect postmarket monitoring to also assess human-AI team performance, workflow effects, near misses, overrides, escalation behavior, and downstream clinical outcomes.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment asks that postmarket evaluation measure human-AI team performance and clinician overrides rather than device output performance alone.
gap_explanations.operational_harm: It calls for monitoring workflow effects, near misses, and escalation behavior, which are operational rather than purely output-accuracy harms.

positions.public_summary: Supports the three proposed postmarket approaches but argues they are complementary, not interchangeable, and that re-benchmarking alone is not clinical performance evaluation. Asks FDA to also expect monitoring of human-AI team performance, workflow effects, near misses, overrides, escalation, and clinical outcomes, scaled to criticality.
positions.source_passage: I support periodic re-benchmarking, clinician review, and degradation monitoring, but consider them complementary rather than interchangeable approaches. Re-benchmarking alone should not be equated with postmarket clinical performance evaluation. ... Depending on criticality, postmarket monitoring should therefore also evaluate aspects such as human-AI team performance, workflow effects, near misses, overrides, escalation behavior, and downstream clinical outcomes.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that static or point-in-time evaluation methods may not adequately capture GenAI device behavior, which unfolds across multi-turn interactions, evolving clinical information, and varying deployment conditions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add dynamic evaluation approaches—multi-turn scenarios, evolving clinical information, simulated or real user interactions, and assessment under changing deployment conditions—to the set of postmarket performance evaluation methods CDRH considers.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment calls for assessment under changing deployment conditions, implying that performance assurance must account for variation across real-world deployment settings over time.

positions.public_summary: Suggests CDRH broaden postmarket performance evaluation beyond the listed approaches to include dynamic methods—multi-turn scenarios, evolving clinical information, simulated or real user interactions, and assessment under changing deployment conditions—as particularly useful for GenAI-enabled devices.
positions.source_passage: Dynamic evaluation approaches may be particularly useful for GenAI-enabled devices. These could include multi-turn scenarios, evolving clinical information, simulated or real user interactions, and assessment under changing deployment conditions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Periodic reassessment alone may not detect emerging performance problems; the commenter is concerned that changes in deployment context, input distributions, underlying models, or the validity of original risk assumptions can invalidate prior evaluations between scheduled reviews.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a postmarket reassessment model that is both periodic and trigger-based, with triggers including adverse events and near misses, drift in inputs, interaction patterns or subgroup performance, invalidated risk-stratification assumptions, changes in workflows, users, guidelines or standards of care, changes to foundation models or components, and unexpected device-clinician-supervisory disagreement.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The commenter treats changes in clinical workflows, user populations, guidelines, and other deployment-environment parameters as reassessment triggers, extending monitoring beyond the device itself to its local deployment context.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: Changes to foundation models or other supplied components are listed as explicit triggers for reassessment, implying ongoing surveillance of upstream component providers.

positions.public_summary: Recommends that postmarket reassessment be both periodic and trigger-based, listing triggers such as adverse events and near misses, drift in inputs or subgroup performance, invalidated risk-stratification assumptions, changes in workflows, users or guidelines, foundation model or component changes, and device-clinician disagreement patterns.
positions.source_passage: Reassessment should be both periodic and trigger-based. Relevant triggers may include: • predefined time intervals; • adverse events, complaints, near misses, or deterioration of risk- or performance-related metrics; • changes in input distributions, interaction patterns, subgroup performance, or other logging-based signals; • indications that assumptions or safeguards underlying the Criticality Stratification are no longer valid; • changes in clinical workflows, user populations, guidelines, standards of care, or other deployment-environment parameters; • changes to foundation models or other components; and • major technological advances or unexpected disagreement patterns between the device, clinicians, and supervisory systems.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that postmarket monitoring focused on a fixed benchmark would miss multiple forms of drift—data, model/component, concept or clinical, workflow/use, and oversight drift—and that an unchanged benchmark may itself become unrepresentative or clinically invalid over time.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand postmarket performance evaluation to explicitly cover the several enumerated drift types, and require that periodic reassessment evaluate whether the benchmark remains representative and clinically valid, not only whether the device continues to pass it.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment identifies workflow/use drift as a monitored dimension, pointing to changes in real deployment conditions rather than model performance alone.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: By naming 'oversight drift' as a form of drift to monitor, the comment treats degradation of human supervision as part of ongoing system performance.

positions.public_summary: Supports postmarket performance evaluation but urges broader scope: monitoring should cover data, model/component, clinical, workflow/use, and oversight drift, and periodic reassessment should test whether the benchmark itself remains representative and clinically valid, not just whether the device still passes it.
positions.source_passage: Postmarket monitoring should address multiple forms of drift, including data drift, model/component drift, concept or clinical drift, workflow/use drift, and oversight drift. Importantly, reassessment should also determine whether the benchmark itself remains representative and clinically valid rather than merely whether the device continues to pass an unchanged benchmark.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Machine-based supervisory agents could make postmarket monitoring more scalable and responsive, but an unvalidated supervisor performing a safety-relevant function could itself fail, especially if it shares foundation models, training sources, or architectures with the monitored device and therefore shares blind spots.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that supervisory agents undergo fit-for-purpose validation and ongoing surveillance, with evaluation criteria including sensitivity to relevant failure modes, robustness, and reproducibility, and apply particular caution when device and supervisor are technically correlated.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment frames automated supervision as a way to scale continuous postmarket evaluation while noting the assurance burden this shifts onto the monitoring layer itself.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It addresses delegating a safety-relevant oversight function to a machine agent and argues that agent must itself be validated and surveilled, especially where it is not independent of the device it supervises.

positions.public_summary: Supports machine-based supervisory agents as potentially improving scalability and responsiveness of postmarket monitoring, but conditions this on the supervisor itself receiving fit-for-purpose validation and ongoing surveillance, with added caution when supervisor and device share foundation models, training sources, or architectures.
positions.source_passage: Machine-based supervisory agents could improve the scalability and responsiveness of postmarket monitoring and may be particularly useful for continuous or dynamic evaluation. However, any supervisory agent performing a safety-relevant monitoring function should itself be subject to fit-for-purpose validation and ongoing surveillance. ... Relevant considerations for the use of machine-based supervisory agents may include sensitivity to relevant failure modes, robustness, reproducibility, and susceptibility to specific failure modes. ... Particular caution may be warranted where the device and supervisor rely on the same or closely related foundation models, training sources, or technical architectures.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Automated supervisory agents may miss novel or unanticipated failure modes they were not designed to detect, so relying on them as a closed automated control loop could leave gaps in postmarket oversight, especially for higher-criticality devices.
positions.requested_fda_action: Treat machine-based supervision as one layer within a broader monitoring architecture and expect periodic qualified human review to be retained, particularly for higher-criticality devices and for detecting unanticipated failure modes.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment addresses how much monitoring authority can be delegated to an automated supervisory agent and argues against a fully closed automated control loop without human review.

positions.public_summary: Accepts machine-based supervisory agents but only as one layer of postmarket monitoring, not a fully closed automated control loop. Urges FDA to expect continued periodic qualified human review, especially for higher-criticality devices and for failure modes automated supervisors were not designed to detect.
positions.source_passage: Machine-based supervision should generally form one layer of a broader monitoring system rather than becoming a fully closed automated control loop. Periodic qualified human review should remain part of the monitoring architecture, particularly for higher-criticality devices and for detecting novel or unanticipated failure modes that an automated supervisor was not designed to identify.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees that clinicians, institutions, professional societies, and standards bodies can supply valuable postmarket information, but is concerned that distributing data collection across the ecosystem could dilute responsibility for acting on it.
positions.requested_fda_action: Structure stakeholder participation in postmarket monitoring so that the manufacturer remains responsible for defining the monitoring strategy, integrating ecosystem-derived information, and implementing corrective and preventive actions.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter draws an explicit line between distributed data collection and distributed accountability, specifying which duties (monitoring strategy, information integration, CAPA) must remain with the manufacturer.

positions.public_summary: Agrees that clinicians, institutions, professional societies, and standards bodies can contribute postmarket monitoring information, but states that distributed data collection must not dilute accountability. Asks FDA to keep manufacturers responsible for monitoring strategy, integrating ecosystem information, and corrective and preventive actions.
positions.source_passage: I agree that clinicians, healthcare institutions, professional societies, standards organizations, and other stakeholders may provide important information for postmarket monitoring ... However, distributed data collection should not result in distributed accountability. The manufacturer should remain responsible for defining the monitoring strategy, integrating relevant information from the ecosystem, and implementing necessary corrective or preventive actions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Changes in the local deployment environment—workflow, local protocols, user qualifications, and the extent or effectiveness of human oversight—may go undetected unless deploying institutions are explicitly engaged, and professional societies are positioned to flag shifts in clinical standards and reference standards.
positions.requested_fda_action: Clearly define the interfaces and responsibilities among manufacturers, deploying healthcare institutions, and professional societies, including through appropriate agreements, and provide for structured manufacturer-institution information exchange mechanisms for higher-criticality applications.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment centers on detecting post-deployment changes in local workflow, protocols, and user qualifications that fall outside the manufacturer's direct visibility.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: It calls for clearly defined interfaces, responsibilities, and agreements across manufacturers, institutions, and professional societies rather than a single accountable party.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It identifies changes in the extent and effectiveness of human oversight as a monitored variable affecting device performance in use.

positions.public_summary: Endorses shared postmarket roles but asks FDA to specify them: institutions should track changes in workflow, local protocols, user qualifications, and human oversight; societies should flag shifts in clinical standards. Requests clearly defined responsibilities, agreements, and structured manufacturer-institution information exchange for higher-criticality uses.
positions.source_passage: Healthcare institutions may have an especially important role in identifying changes in the deployment environment, including workflow modifications, local protocols, user qualifications, and changes in the extent or effectiveness of human oversight. The associated interfaces and responsibilities should be clearly defined, including through appropriate agreements where applicable. Professional societies may contribute to identifying changes in clinical standards, guidelines, and appropriate reference standards. For higher-criticality applications, structured mechanisms for information exchange between manufacturers and deploying institutions may therefore be appropriate.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Scaling reassessment to the technical magnitude of a change may miss modifications that are technically small but affect safety-critical competencies, human-oversight mechanisms, boundary behavior, or clinical decision pathways, and may overlook the combined effect of multiple minor changes.
positions.requested_fda_action: Accept the premarket competency assessment as a baseline, but scale re-benchmarking according to a change's potential impact on competencies, criticality, safeguards, clinical performance, and the validity of original evaluation assumptions, and require consideration of cumulative change; allow well-characterized, bounded changes to remain within the quality management system.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The comment notes that multiple individually minor modifications can cumulatively produce a substantially different device or deployment configuration, a drift in the device's behavioral envelope not addressed by change-by-change review.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It identifies changes affecting human-oversight mechanisms and clinical decision pathways as triggers for substantial reassessment, framing the human-device system rather than the model alone as the object of evaluation.

positions.public_summary: Accepts the premarket competency assessment as a baseline for evaluating modifications, but argues reassessment scope should track potential impact on competencies, criticality, safeguards, oversight mechanisms, and original evaluation assumptions rather than technical magnitude, and should account for cumulative minor changes.
positions.source_passage: In principle, the premarket competency-based assessment can serve as a baseline for evaluating post-deployment modifications, as proposed by the Discussion Paper. However, the scope of reassessment should depend not merely on the technical magnitude of a change, but on its potential impact on competencies, criticality, safeguards, clinical performance, and the validity of the original evaluation assumptions. A seemingly small technical modification may warrant substantial reassessment if it affects a safety-critical competency, human-oversight mechanism, boundary behavior, or clinical decision pathway. Conversely, some changes may reasonably remain within the quality management system if their potential impact is well characterized and bounded. Reassessment should also consider cumulative change. Multiple individually minor modifications may collectively produce a substantially different device or deployment configuration.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Post-modification evaluation could overstate performance if clinical cases are assessed with information that would not have been available to the device at the actual decision point.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should expect post-change evaluations to preserve temporal fidelity by restricting device inputs to information available at the relevant decision point, while permitting later-acquired information to be used for establishing the reference standard.
positions.public_summary: Comment addresses methodology for re-evaluating devices after modifications, asking FDA to require temporal fidelity: cases should be assessed using only information available at the decision point, with later-acquired information used only to establish the reference standard.
positions.source_passage: Where relevant, post-change evaluation should preserve temporal fidelity: clinical cases should be evaluated using only information that would have been available at the relevant decision point, while later information may appropriately contribute to establishing the reference standard.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter accepts PCCPs as a suitable mechanism for GenAI-enabled devices but notes that the exact nature of future modifications may not be fully predictable, limiting the feasibility of exhaustive technical prespecification.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adapt PCCP concepts for GenAI so they rely more on procedural and boundary-based prespecification (defining permissible limits and processes for change) rather than requiring detailed technical specification of every anticipated modification.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The suggestion to prespecify boundaries rather than specific modifications implies governing an evolving behavioral envelope rather than a fixed, fully enumerated change list.

positions.public_summary: Supports extending PCCPs to GenAI-enabled devices, but argues future modifications cannot be fully predicted. Recommends that GenAI PCCPs rely more on procedural and boundary-based prespecification than on exhaustive technical prespecification of each anticipated change.
positions.source_passage: PCCPs are an important approach for AI-enabled devices and it is reasonable to extend this concept to GenAI-enabled systems. However, it should be recognized that the exact nature of all future modifications may not be fully predictable. For GenAI, PCCPs may therefore need to rely more heavily on procedural and boundary-based prespecification rather than exhaustive technical prespecification of every future modification.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the competency-based approach as a useful basis for change control but considers current PCCP approaches too narrow to govern devices that may move toward greater operational independence over time.
positions.requested_fda_action: Extend PCCP concepts so that they define staged progression from restricted or closely supervised use toward greater operational independence, permitting advancement only when predefined competency and real-world performance criteria are met, and allowing downgrading of scope, autonomy, or supervision requirements when postmarket signals emerge.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment proposes that a device's level of operational independence and required human supervision be granted, and withdrawn, based on demonstrated competency and real-world performance rather than fixed at authorization.
gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: It contemplates a device's authorized scope and autonomy shifting up or down over the deployment lifecycle in response to performance signals, which the PCCP question does not fully frame.

positions.public_summary: Supports using the competency-based approach for PCCPs but asks FDA to extend it into staged authorization: advancement from supervised use toward greater operational independence only after predefined competency and real-world performance criteria are met, with downgrading of scope, autonomy, or supervision if postmarket signals emerge.
positions.source_passage: The competency-based approach could provide a useful but extended structure for such PCCPs. In comparison to currently pursued PCCP approaches, the stages from restricted or closely supervised use toward greater operational independence may be integrated into this approach. Progression between these stages should occur only when predefined competency and real-world performance criteria have been met. Conversely, emerging postmarket signals may lead to a downgrading, such as reducing scope or autonomy or increasing required human supervision.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A device can remain technically unchanged while external conditions—new clinical guidelines, workflows, or user competencies—invalidate the assumptions underlying its original evaluation, leaving change-control approaches focused only on model modifications incomplete.
positions.requested_fda_action: Extend PCCP and change-control concepts to address environmental change, including periodic reassessment of whether the original evaluation framework and its underlying assumptions remain valid.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The comment notes that the validity of a device's prior assessment can lapse without any change to the device, as evolving guidelines and use contexts shift the assumptions defining its evaluated envelope.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It points to deployment-side factors such as workflows and user competencies as determinants of continued assurance, which manufacturer-centered change control does not track.

positions.public_summary: Supports PCCP-based change control but argues it should extend beyond device modifications: because new clinical guidelines, workflows, or user competencies can invalidate assumptions behind a prior assessment even when the device is unchanged, PCCPs should address environmental change and continued evaluation-framework validity.
positions.source_passage: PCCPs should also account for changes in the environment and the continued validity of the evaluation framework. A device may remain technically unchanged while new clinical guidelines, workflows, user competencies, or other environmental factors invalidate assumptions underlying its prior assessment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Changes to an underlying foundation model may alter clinical performance, user interaction, and behavior in the deployment environment, and may invalidate the competency level assumed at authorization.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that postmarket monitoring strategies explicitly assess foundation model changes, including targeted benchmarking of clinical performance and effects on user interaction and deployment environment, and provide that major changes trigger a downgrade in assumed competency, a return to greater supervision, and a requalification period until defined evidence gates are passed.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment treats upstream foundation model changes as a supplier-driven risk that must be continuously monitored and re-evaluated rather than assumed stable.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It asks that reassessment after model changes cover effects on the interaction between the device and its users, not only standalone model output.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It proposes returning the device to a more controlled, supervised deployment stage with staged evidence gates before independent use is restored.

positions.public_summary: Supports postmarket attention to third-party model changes but asks FDA to go further: require explicit assessment of foundation model changes, including benchmarking of clinical performance, user interaction, and deployment environment, with major changes triggering competency downgrade, renewed supervision, and requalification via defined evidence gates.
positions.source_passage: An assessment of changes in the underlying foundation models should be included explicitly in the postmarket monitoring strategy. This may include specific benchmarking tests to assess the impact of changes in the foundation model on resulting clinical performance. Additionally, these steps should address effects on the interaction between the GenAI-enabled device and users as well as the deployment environment. ... Major changes in foundation models or other components may necessitate a downgrading of the currently assumed competency level. The GenAI-enabled device may need to return to a stage with greater supervision. This would amount to a requalification period in a more controlled environment. A more independent use of the GenAI system can be re-established when defined evidence gates are successfully passed.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without the ability to reconstruct the configuration in effect at the time of a given use, manufacturers cannot meaningfully investigate complaints, adverse events, or performance signals for devices whose behavior depends on shifting foundation-model versions, prompts, retrieval sources, tools, and runtime settings.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add a case-level reconstructability requirement: manufacturers should retain sufficient traceability of historical system configuration (foundation-model version, prompts, guardrails, retrieval/knowledge-base version, tools, orchestration logic, runtime parameters, clinical-environment information) to permit reliable investigation and reassessment of safety-critical behavior, acknowledging that exact reproduction of stochastic outputs may not be feasible.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment ties investigability to versioned traceability of third-party supplied components such as foundation-model versions, retrieval sources, and tools.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It focuses on capturing the as-deployed configuration and clinical-environment context at the time of each use rather than a single premarket configuration.

positions.public_summary: Supports FDA's direction on third-party model change control but asks that it add a case-level reconstructability requirement: manufacturers should retain traceable records of model version, prompts, guardrails, retrieval sources, tools, and runtime settings at time of use, acknowledging stochastic outputs may not be exactly reproducible.
positions.source_passage: An additional requirement should be case-level reconstructability. For meaningful investigation of complaints, adverse events, or performance signals, the manufacturer should be able to reconstruct, to the extent technically feasible, the relevant device configuration at the time of use. This may include the foundation-model version, prompts, guardrails, retrieval sources or knowledge-base version, tools, orchestration logic, relevant runtime parameters, and applicable clinical-environment information. Exact reproduction of every stochastic output may not always be feasible. Nevertheless, the historical system configuration should remain sufficiently traceable to permit reliable investigation and reassessment of safety-critical behavior.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that treating postmarket surveillance as periodic performance checks is inadequate for GenAI devices, and that the pace of technological and operational change could outstrip the capacity of monitoring and regulatory systems to detect, understand, and control its consequences.
positions.requested_fda_action: Frame postmarket monitoring as an active, continuous lifecycle control system rather than periodic reassessment, and constrain the permitted rate of technological and operational change so it remains within the detection and control capability of the monitoring and regulatory system.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment ties allowable change to the practical capacity of monitoring and regulatory systems to detect and control consequences, raising a scalability limit on assurance not addressed by FDA's questions.
gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: It treats ongoing technological and operational change as something that must be bounded over the device lifecycle, implying a need to constrain the evolving behavioral envelope rather than only re-evaluate discrete modifications.

positions.public_summary: Supports greater postmarket emphasis but urges FDA to treat monitoring as an active lifecycle control system rather than periodic performance checks, and to limit the permitted rate of technological and operational change to what monitoring and regulatory systems can detect, understand, and control.
positions.source_passage: Overall, postmarket monitoring for GenAI-enabled devices should be understood as an active lifecycle control system rather than a periodic performance check. ... Importantly, the rate of permitted technological and operational change should remain compatible with the ability of the monitoring and regulatory system to detect, understand, and control its consequences.

positions.stakeholder_concern: In agentic architectures, the technical cause of failure, operational control, and regulatory responsibility can become separated across device manufacturers, foundation model providers, agent/orchestration providers, and healthcare institutions, whereas existing frameworks assume a single identifiable responsible manufacturer.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should ensure accountability is not diffused across the ecosystem by requiring a clearly defined party responsible for the safety and effectiveness of the end-to-end system, underpinned by contractual, technical, and quality-management arrangements among the participating parties.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The passage argues that fault, control, and regulatory responsibility can separate across multiple parties in agentic systems, requiring an explicit assignment of end-to-end responsibility rather than diffusion.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: It calls for contractual, technical, and quality-management arrangements among device manufacturers, foundation model providers, and orchestration providers to underpin accountability.

positions.public_summary: Notes that in agentic architectures, failure causes, operational control, and regulatory responsibility may be split among device manufacturers, foundation model and orchestration providers, and health systems. Urges FDA to require clearly assigned end-to-end responsibility, supported by contractual, technical, and quality-management arrangements, rather than diffused accountability.
positions.source_passage: Existing medical device regulatory frameworks rely on an identifiable manufacturer or sponsor being responsible for the safety and effectiveness of the device. In agentic architectures, however, the technical cause of a failure, operational control over the relevant component, and regulatory responsibility may become separated across the device manufacturers, foundation model providers, agent or orchestration providers, and healthcare institutions. Nevertheless, accountability should not simply be diffused across the ecosystem. Rather, there should be a clearly defined responsibility for the safety and effectiveness of the end-to-end system, supported by appropriate contractual, technical, and quality-management arrangements among the parties involved.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic devices that autonomously plan and execute multi-step tasks, use external tools, and act across multiple system components create system-level risks that make attribution and control of safety-critical failures substantially harder than for individual GenAI functions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that risk contributions arising across components and interfaces be assessed and managed at the level of the overall system, including through product-specific risk management and criticality stratification.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment states that autonomous action across multiple components and interfaces makes attribution of safety-critical failures substantially more difficult, implying responsibility is spread across system elements.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It emphasizes that devices autonomously planning and executing multi-step tasks and invoking external tools raise control problems beyond those of individual GenAI functions.

positions.public_summary: Agrees that agentic GenAI devices raise considerations beyond non-agentic ones, noting autonomous multi-step action and tool use complicate attribution and control of safety-critical failures. Asks FDA to require system-level risk assessment across components and interfaces, using product-specific risk management and criticality stratification.
positions.source_passage: Agentic GenAI-enabled devices introduce additional system-level risks that go beyond those associated with individual GenAI-enabled functions. In particular, their ability to autonomously plan and execute multi-step tasks, interact with external tools, and take actions across multiple system components can make both the attribution and control of safety-critical failures substantially more difficult. ... Risk contributions may arise across components and interfaces and therefore need to be assessed and managed at the level of the overall system, including through Product-Specific Risk Management and Criticality Stratification.

positions.stakeholder_concern: In multi-step agentic workflows, an erroneous output can become an input to later steps, trigger further tool calls, and amplify the original error, so evaluating components in isolation may miss compounding failures, especially for irreversible or high-consequence actions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require premarket evaluation to extend beyond individual agents, models, or tools to representative end-to-end workflows, including safety-critical interaction pathways, foreseeable failure combinations, recovery behavior, and escalation to human oversight, with particular attention to irreversible or high-consequence actions.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The comment focuses on harm arising from error propagation and amplification across chained workflow steps and tool calls rather than from a single incorrect output.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It asks that evaluation cover recovery behavior and escalation to human oversight as part of the workflow, not just standalone model performance.

positions.public_summary: Addressing agentic devices, the commenter urges FDA to go beyond evaluating individual agents, models, or tools and require premarket assessment of representative end-to-end workflows—covering error propagation across steps, safety-critical pathways, foreseeable failure combinations, recovery behavior, and human escalation—especially for irreversible or high-consequence actions.
positions.source_passage: A second consideration is failure propagation within multi-step workflows. An erroneous output in one step may become the input to subsequent steps, trigger additional tool calls, or result in actions that further amplify the original error. Premarket evaluation should therefore not only assess individual agents, models, or tools, but also representative end-to-end workflows, including safety-critical interaction pathways, foreseeable failure combinations, recovery behavior, and escalation to human oversight. This is particularly important for irreversible or high-consequence actions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic systems dynamically select tools and alter task sequences across a very large state space, so component-level or exhaustive combinatorial testing cannot demonstrate end-to-end safety. Responsibility for integration-level evidence may be ambiguous when components come from multiple providers.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require system-level evaluation based on risk-based coverage of safety-relevant configurations and representative interaction trajectories, paired with postmarket monitoring able to detect previously unobserved failure patterns. Clearly allocate integration-testing responsibility, with the party responsible for the final user-facing device ensuring sufficient end-to-end evidence.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment addresses how evidence responsibilities should be divided between component providers and the party fielding the final user-facing device, with the latter accountable for end-to-end evidence.
gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: It highlights that agentic behavior emerges from dynamic tool selection and altered task sequences across many possible states, making a fixed, fully pre-specified testable behavioral envelope infeasible.

positions.public_summary: Comment on agentic devices: supports evaluation but urges system-level rather than component-focused testing, arguing exhaustive combination testing is infeasible. Recommends risk-based coverage of safety-relevant configurations and representative interaction trajectories plus postmarket detection of new failure patterns, with the final device party ensuring end-to-end evidence.
positions.source_passage: Accordingly, testing should address system-level behavior rather than primarily focusing on individual components. Such testing will, however, be particularly challenging because agentic systems may dynamically select tools, alter task sequences, and operate across a large number of possible system states. Comprehensive testing of all combinations is unlikely to be feasible. Evaluation should therefore focus on risk-based coverage of safety-relevant configurations and representative interaction trajectories, complemented by postmarket monitoring capable of identifying previously unobserved failure patterns. ... Responsibilities for integration testing should be clearly allocated. Component providers may supply evidence for their components, but the party responsible for the final user-facing device should ensure that end-to-end evidence is sufficient.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that agentic GenAI systems depend on interoperability at multiple levels—technical exchange of data and commands, consistent semantic interpretation of clinical concepts, units, timestamps, uncertainty, patient context, and workflow states, and governance alignment. Without these, responsibilities for risk management, change control, validation, monitoring, and corrective action across organizational boundaries remain undefined.
positions.requested_fda_action: Recognize interoperability as an additional consideration for agentic devices, addressing technical and semantic interoperability among participating agents and tools, and establish governance and regulatory alignment that assigns risk management, change control, validation, monitoring, and corrective action responsibilities across organizations.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment emphasizes that responsibilities for risk management, change control, validation, monitoring, and corrective actions must be defined across organizational boundaries in agentic systems.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It identifies semantic consistency across interacting agents, tools, and workflow states as a prerequisite for reliable operation in real deployment environments, beyond the device-level framing of Q26.

positions.public_summary: Responding on agentic systems, the commenter adds interoperability as an additional consideration: technical data and command exchange, semantic consistency in interpreting clinical concepts, units, timestamps, uncertainty, context, and workflow state, plus governance defining risk management, change control, validation, monitoring, and corrective-action responsibilities across organizations.
positions.source_passage: In addition, agentic systems require interoperability at several levels. Technical interoperability is necessary to ensure reliable exchange of data and commands, but is not sufficient. Semantic interoperability is also critical: participating agents and tools need to interpret clinical concepts, units, timestamps, uncertainty, patient context, and workflow states consistently. Finally, appropriate governance and regulatory alignment are required to define responsibilities for risk management, change control, validation, monitoring, and corrective actions across organizational boundaries.

positions.stakeholder_concern: As agentic devices take autonomous multi-step actions with less direct human review, acceptance criteria and oversight must account for tool failures, containment of errors, and the ability to return control to humans. Monitoring only individual components would miss changes in how the overall agentic system behaves in interaction.
positions.requested_fda_action: Apply progressively stricter acceptance criteria as autonomy and potential harm severity increase, including predefined human-oversight checkpoints for high-consequence actions, handling of erroneous or unavailable tools, traceability, failure containment, and demonstrated safe-state reversion or deferral to human control. Extend postmarket oversight to system-level interaction behavior, not just component performance.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The comment focuses on failure modes such as erroneous or unavailable tools, failure containment, and safe-state reversion, which are operational system failures beyond clinical output accuracy.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It calls for predefined human-oversight checkpoints for high-consequence actions and demonstrated ability to defer to human control, addressing how much action authority is delegated to the device.
gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: It asks that postmarket oversight track changes in interaction behavior across the overall agentic system, not just fixed component performance.

positions.public_summary: Supports FDA's attention to agentic devices but urges acceptance criteria that tighten progressively with autonomy and harm severity, specifying human-oversight checkpoints, tool-failure handling, traceability, failure containment, and safe-state reversion, plus postmarket monitoring of system-level interaction behavior, not only individual components.
positions.source_passage: Finally, the reduced opportunity for direct human review should be reflected in progressively stricter acceptance criteria as autonomy and potential severity of harm increase. Such criteria could include predefined human-oversight checkpoints for high-consequence actions, reliable detection and handling of erroneous or unavailable tools, traceability of relevant decisions and actions, effective containment of failures, and demonstrated ability to revert to a safe state or defer to human control. Postmarket oversight should similarly address not only performance of individual components, but also changes in interaction behavior across the overall agentic system.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that initial regulatory stratification by criticality may be conflated with product-specific risk management, and that a framework could treat technological novelty as a proxy for risk rather than assessing the final user-facing device in its intended use environment.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a risk-proportionate, lifecycle-based framework that clearly separates initial regulatory stratification (setting oversight and evidence levels) from product-specific risk management and evaluation, and keep the framework adaptive to open-ended behavior, evolving foundation models, human-AI interaction, and agentic functions.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The comment asks the framework to remain adaptive to open-ended behavior, evolving foundation models, and agentic functions, which the two-axis risk framing does not fully capture.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It states that evaluation should establish assurance for the final user-facing device in its intended use environment, including human-AI interaction, rather than the model alone.

positions.public_summary: Supports a risk-proportionate, lifecycle-based approach but asks FDA to clearly separate initial regulatory stratification by criticality from product-specific risk management, which should assess the user-facing device in its intended use environment, and to remain adaptive without equating novelty with risk.
positions.source_passage: Taken together, these comments support a risk-proportionate and lifecycle-based regulatory approach that clearly distinguishes the initial regulatory stratification of a device from Product-Specific Risk Management. Criticality should help determine the level of oversight and evidence, while Product-Specific Risk Management and evaluation should establish whether the final user-facing device, in its intended use environment, provides reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness. At the same time, the framework should remain sufficiently adaptive to address open-ended behavior, evolving foundation models, human-AI interaction, and agentic functions without treating technological novelty itself as a proxy for risk.
